solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Piece wife's getting fried?

indicators.note: the wife is getting into the frying vessel, so her letter goes inside the other piece

parts.note: something fried is cooked in a pan
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A cookery mishap: someone's wife ends up frying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' looks like a slice of food in the kitchen scene, but it is a chess piece.
explanation.definitionFit: The humblest chessman on the board is one of the pieces of the game.

clue.text: 'Obnoxious' about right for 'smug'

indicators.note: the word for obnoxious goes about, i.e. around, the letter for right

parts.note: piggish behaviour is greedy and obnoxious

explanation.surface: A quibble over vocabulary: is 'obnoxious' about right as a substitute for 'smug'?
explanation.definitionFit: Someone self-righteous and prim is smug, priding themselves on their own virtue.

clue.text: Old spoken ruling written up for Australian native

indicators.note: in a down clue, written up means the letters are read from the bottom, i.e. backwards

parts.note: oral means spoken
a law is a ruling

explanation.surface: A historian notes an ancient oral law being finally committed to writing, applying to Australia's original people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Australian native' suggests an Aboriginal people, but it is an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a kind of large kangaroo found in Australia, a native animal of that continent.

clue.text: Near thing becomes near ting? Be careful about it

indicators.note: the Latin warning goes about, i.e. around, the description of what happens to the word

parts.note: cave (Latin 'beware') is a schoolboy's warning to be careful
the phrase 'near thing' turns into 'near ting' when it loses its H, so this describes it as LOSES H

explanation.surface: A pedantic note on accents: dropping an H turns one phrase into another, so watch out.
explanation.walkthrough: CAVE is Latin for 'beware', schoolboy slang in Britain. 'it' simply refers back to the H-dropping description.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow escape is called a near thing, and also a close call of this razor-edge sort.

clue.text: Sprawl around, say, in European province

indicators.note: the word for sprawl goes around the abbreviation for say

parts.note: to sprawl is to lie stretched out
e.g. (for example) is a common way of saying 'say'

explanation.surface: Someone lounges around on holiday in some province of Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a province in eastern Belgium, so a European administrative region.

clue.text: Classic film role in the bag, American

indicators.note: the word for role is placed in the word for bag

parts.note: a sac is a bag, as in a biological pouch
an actor's part is a role

explanation.surface: An American actor has landed a role in a classic film, the part in the bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classic film role' looks like one phrase, but the definition stops at 'film' and 'role' is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1960 Kubrick epic about the rebel gladiator is a classic Hollywood picture.

clue.text: Pass round untidy semi, seeking dope

indicators.note: the name of the Alpine pass goes round the scrambled letters

parts.note: the Simplon is a famous Alpine pass between Switzerland and Italy

indicators.note: an untidy thing is jumbled, so the letters of semi are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone hands round drugs in a messy semi-detached house, looking for dope.
explanation.walkthrough: A semi is a British semi-detached house; 'dope' means a fool here, not drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme simpleton who met a pieman is a byword for a fool, or dope.

clue.text: Reluctant to help, supporting gaffer regularly

indicators.note: in a down clue the help word sits beneath, supporting, the letters above it
regularly takes every other letter of the word gaffer, starting from its second

parts.note: aid means help

explanation.surface: An assistant is reluctant to help, though propping up the boss now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reluctant to help' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'Reluctant'. 'regularly' takes AFR from gaffer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being frightened of doing something makes a person reluctant to do it, as in 'I'm loath to'.

clue.text: Tribute union of nations added to record, ultimate in bravery

indicators.note: the final letter is added to the end of what precedes it

parts.note: the EU is the European Union, a union of nations
a log is a record, as kept by a ship

indicators.note: ultimate in picks the last letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A tribute to a union of nations goes on record, celebrating its bravery.
explanation.definitionFit: A speech of praise, often at a funeral, is a spoken tribute to someone.

clue.text: Slow getting back into panel discussion

indicators.note: getting back says the concealed letters are read backwards
into says the letters are buried within the words panel discussion

explanation.surface: A panel debate has gone sluggish, and someone tries to rejoin it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' finds ELDI across 'panel discussion'; 'getting back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine that runs slowly while not engaged idles, so the verb means run slow.

clue.text: Delicate winger transferred from Real Madrid

indicators.note: the letters are transferred, i.e. moved about, from the club's name into a new order

explanation.surface: Football gossip: a skilful winger has been transferred from Real Madrid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delicate winger' is a footballer in the surface but a butterfly in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A fragile butterfly has wings, so it is cheekily called a delicate winger.

clue.text: Nobleman's rank retaining name, duke, ultimately

indicators.note: the word for rank holds on to, i.e. retains, the abbreviation for name

parts.note: a grade is a rank

indicators.note: ultimately picks the final letter of duke

explanation.surface: A nobleman's title stays in the family until it reaches the rank of duke.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish or Portuguese aristocrat of high rank, and by extension any important noble.

clue.text: Next to nothing large eclipsed by small, short and thick

indicators.note: the letter for large is covered, eclipsed, by the word for small

parts.note: diddy is British slang for small
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels
squat means short and thick

explanation.surface: A sizing chart's description: large is overshadowed by small, which is short and stocky.
explanation.walkthrough: DIDDY is informal British for small or tiny.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang phrase means nothing at all or very little, as in 'he knows zilch'.

clue.text: Significant relation

definitions.meaning: a ... remark is revealing and significant
a relation is a narration, the recounting of a story

explanation.surface: An important family member.
explanation.definitionFit: Revealing remarks are meaningful, and the recounting of a story is its narration.

clue.text: Change in pounds beats wonga

indicators.note: a change in the word pounds means its letters are reordered

parts.note: licks means beats, as in a thrashing

explanation.surface: A change in the money supply beats payday cash.
explanation.walkthrough: Wonga is British slang for money, as is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal British words for cash or money.

clue.text: Most foolish, anyway

definitions.meaning: the most foolish person has the smallest amount of sense, read as a two-word phrase
a dialect or American adverb meaning at any rate

explanation.surface: Someone is the silliest of the lot, in any case.
explanation.definitionFit: Split in two the word describes whoever has the smallest share of sense; whole, it means at any rate.

clue.text: Risk to make peace, then?

definitions.meaning: to put in danger is to risk
split three and five, the word reads as putting a stop to fury, a step towards peace

explanation.surface: Is it a gamble to try to make peace?
explanation.definitionFit: To expose something to harm is to imperil or risk it; split, it means stopping rage.

clue.text: Gosh, Pygmalion and Animal Farm so?

definitions.meaning: Pygmalion was written ... Bernard Shaw and Animal Farm ... Orwell, so both are authored by a George

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at two classic books.
explanation.definitionFit: Both an exclamation like 'goodness me' and a description of works by two writers named George.

clue.text: Yuppy requiring loan some day when in difficulties

indicators.note: letters in difficulties are in trouble and get thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A young professional needs a loan one day when money gets tight.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a Harry Enfield comic character of 1980s Britain, whose name became slang for a flashy, money-obsessed yuppie.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a brash comedy character came to stand for any showy, wealthy young professional.

clue.text: Number of horses run in sharp practice

indicators.note: the letter for run is put in the word for sharp practice

parts.note: a sting is a confidence trick, sharp practice
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A racing scandal: a bunch of horses running in a crooked scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of racehorses kept by one stable or owner is called by this collective word.

clue.text: Parcels to be put away, obscure problem

parts.note: dim means obscure or faint
a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: A puzzling problem about parcels being stored out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: These Chinese dumplings are little parcels of food, and to put food away is to eat it.

clue.text: Charlie around nose, nothing less, in ladies' outfit

indicators.note: the word for Charlie goes around the shortened nose

parts.note: a charlie is a fool, a twit

indicators.note: less means the following letter is taken away

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A clown with a red nose wears a lady's outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less' takes O from nose to give NSE. A charlie is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A matching jumper and cardigan worn together is a classic women's garment set.

clue.text: Character concealing horse's weight

indicators.note: the word for character hides the horse word within it

parts.note: tone is character or style
a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: A personality hiding a horse's weight.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the carrying capacity or weight of a ship, measured in tons.

clue.text: All fingers and thumbs alternatively making sense

parts.note: fingers and thumbs together number ten
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A clumsy person is told they are, alternatively, making sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All fingers and thumbs' looks like the idiom for clumsy, but simply counts digits.
explanation.definitionFit: The general drift or meaning of a document is its purport, i.e. its sense.

clue.text: Casual suit, edges trimmed, contains bum

indicators.note: bum as an adjective means poor or wrong, so the letters are put into a wrong order
edges trimmed removes the outer letters of suit

explanation.surface: A casual suit, its hems trimmed, has room for a backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bum' looks like a noun, the backside, but works as an adjective meaning faulty, which signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Being carefree and nonchalant is a relaxed, casual attitude.

clue.text: Jelly fish passing barracuda's tail

indicators.note: the letter moves past and sits alongside the fish
the tail of a word is its final letter

parts.note: a gar is a long-snouted fish

explanation.surface: A jellyfish drifts past a barracuda's tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jelly fish' reads as the sea creature, but 'Jelly' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A gelatinous substance from seaweed, used as a culture medium and setting agent.

clue.text: Bloody outstanding article by a setter for analysis in competition

indicators.note: the word for bloody stands outside the rest

parts.note: gory means bloody

indicators.note: the article sits by, next to, the preceding letters

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me
the is the definite article

explanation.surface: A setter boasts of a bloody brilliant article written for a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: The mathematical study of strategic decisions is an analysis of competitive situations.

clue.text: Peter Sellers holds tongue

indicators.note: the actor's name holds the letters within it

explanation.surface: The comic actor Peter Sellers keeps quiet, holding his tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Gaelic language of Scotland or Ireland, and a language is a tongue.
